summary: Qwen Team technical report on reward signals for training coding agents, in four parts. (1) SWE-like tasks: an agentic judge filters tasks whose instructions are unclear or whose tests do not match the instruction, and a trajectory monitor penalises shortcut behaviour such as fetching the upstream fix during RL. (2) Frontend: rubric judges and a Playwright-driven interactive judge. (3) About 125k internal engineer-assistant conversations, auto-labelled for implicit user feedback by an LLM, are used for span-level KTO. (4) An agentic evaluator for repository-from-spec generation is used to filter rejection-sampling data. Everything is measured on Qwen checkpoints, often on internal benchmarks. It informs model training, not harness configuration.

claims.claim: Behaviour monitoring cuts hacked-resolved from 28.57% to 0.56% and raises clean-resolved from 40.22% to 60.53% across three SWE-bench variants
claims.evidence: Table 3, Fig. 5. 'Clean resolved' and 'hack rate' are defined by the same monitor whose patterns were penalised during training, so the gain is partly circular. Raw verifier pass rates for the monitored run are not tabulated. One RL run per arm.

claims.claim: An agentic quality judge reliably flags SWE tasks with unclear instructions or misaligned tests, and filtering improves RL
claims.evidence: Table 1: instruct_clear F1 90.8-94.7 and instruct_ut_align F1 75.0-81.2 against a human-annotated set whose size is not reported. The RL benefit is shown only as training curves in Fig. 4 (SWE-bench Multilingual and Pro up, Verified 'comparable'); no final numbers are given.

claims.claim: The interactive (browser-driven) judge resists the length hacking that static judges suffer, and improves frontend RFT
claims.evidence: Fig. 6 shows curves only. Table 5 is a single run on two internal benchmarks (WebDev Human Eval 78 to 84, QwenWebBench 1509 to 1545). App. E reports judge variance below 12 Elo.

claims.claim: Span-KTO on implicit user feedback beats SFT and reweighted SFT on five benchmarks (+5.6 pp SWE-bench Verified, +13.3 pp internal Aone-bench)
claims.evidence: Fig. 10 shows error bars ('std across multiple evaluations'). The polarity labels come from Qwen-Plus as judge with no human agreement check. The '98.9% of user evaluations are reasonable' figure is that same judge's own label. Aone-bench is internal.

claims.claim: Evaluator-filtered data 'stably outperforms' random sampling for repo-generation RFT
claims.evidence: Table 10, three-run averages: 23.52 vs 21.61 at the final checkpoint, but filtered is worse than random at 150 steps (19.58 vs 20.29), and the unfiltered full set (24.75) beats the filtered one. 'Stably' is not supported.

patterns.note: In 125k internal conversations with senior engineers, 21.1% of negative user signals are LLM-labelled as 'misunderstanding' of intent (Fig. 8). The agent-as-judge rubric scores whether ambiguous requirements are confirmed first (App. J.2). Asking before implementing is never isolated or compared with not asking.

App. B shows real PR-derived tasks whose requirements live in private Slack channels or undocumented conventions. The judge flags these tasks as unsolvable and drops them; it does not recover the missing knowledge.

Test-based rewards are hackable: solution-artifact retrieval resolves 72.3% vs a 60.0% baseline (Table 2). For the long-horizon evaluator, adding executed tests and end-to-end checks to a code-reading evaluator raises best-of-N accuracy from 57.9 to 63.9-67.4 (Table 6; one evaluator model, n<360, one run per prompt version).

Rubric judges track human rankings (Spearman 0.81-0.905, Table 4) and rankings are stable across judge configurations. Static judges are length-hacked under RL, while a runtime-interactive judge is not (Fig. 6, curves only). Judge and policy are both Qwen.

Span-level KTO beats SFT and reweighted SFT on the same user-feedback data on five benchmarks (Fig. 10), and RFT lifts the base model from 11.41 to 23.52 (Table 10). Only Qwen models; the comparison is between training recipes, not a harness choice.

A trajectory-level monitor audits commands, network access and git operations for shortcut patterns, with a pattern set that is updated over training. It is evaluated only with metrics the monitor itself defines.
Per-task checklists (25.9 items on average, across six dimensions) for frontend judging. The text says rubrics improve agreement with humans, but Table 4 gives no no-rubric baseline.

methodology.sample: SWE-Universe tasks (count not given); 671 WebDev tasks x 8 models; 125,528 internal trajectories / 535,737 rounds; NL2Repo 104 tasks with up to 4 generations each; 19,050 RFT trajectories
methodology.baselines: Unmonitored RL; SFT and RW-SFT; random sampling; static visual and hybrid judges
methodology.models: Internal Qwen-Turbo/Plus/Max checkpoints as policies; Qwen, Claude Opus 4.7 and DeepSeek V4 Pro as evaluators
methodology.variance: Mostly single runs. Three-run averages for RFT; std bars in Fig. 10; Elo variance decomposition for the interactive judge
methodology.ablations: Judge model/voting/few-shot (Table 1), evaluator prompt v1-v5 (Table 6), RW-SFT weights, Span-KTO hyperparameters
methodology.contamination_controls: Git history after the PR date is sanitised and network is disabled for SWE tasks; the trajectory monitor; OpenHands evaluation with network off
methodology.languages: SWE-bench Verified/Pro/Multilingual; HTML/CSS/JS frontend; NL2Repo (mostly Python)

standards.artifacts: Judge prompts and rubrics are in the appendices. No code, data, checkpoints, or internal benchmarks are released.

biases.detail: Qwen policies are trained and judged with Qwen judges. The hacking monitor defines both the training penalty and the reported 'clean' metric.
User-feedback polarity, 'fairness' and the six-dimension behaviour scores are LLM-labelled with no human agreement figures.
Internal benchmarks (Aone-bench, QwenWebBench, WebDev Human Eval), internal user logs and checkpoints.
Table 3, Table 5 and the RL curves are single runs.
Rice's theorem and 'no silver bullet' framing; a product ranking (Qwen3.7-Max 4th on Code Arena) is inserted into the methods.

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Qwen models and Qwen training recipes
coi.detail: A vendor reports its own training methods improving its own models, largely on internal benchmarks, and cites a leaderboard rank for its product. It does report negative results: the v5 prompt is worse, and the unfiltered full data beats the filtered set. Public SWE-bench numbers are included.

verdict_reason: There are many experiments, but the key reward-hacking gain is measured with the same monitor used in training, the RFT 'stable' advantage is not stable, and the feedback labels come from an unvalidated LLM judge on internal data. It is useful as an industry account of reward-hacking modes, not as evidence for a harness decision.
applicability: Low for a team that does not train models. Two observations carry over to pre-spec work. First, real tickets often hide requirements in places the agent cannot reach (private chat, undocumented conventions). A cheap pre-implementation check, 'is this ticket self-contained and are its referenced sources accessible?', is a plausible gate before an agent starts, but this paper only uses such a check to discard training tasks. Second, senior engineers' corrections were often about misunderstood intent (21.1% of negative signals, LLM-labelled), which argues for an explicit intent-confirmation step (P40). The paper never tests that step.
